sentences.text: These high neural spines likely supported a large muscle ridge along the animal's body, with lower spines attaching powerful muscles similar to modern bison to form a tall, thick ridge.
The animal had an estimated skull length of 1.23 to 1.29 meters and a total body length of 11 to 12 meters.
Its jaws contained nineteen curved, serrated teeth on each side of the upper jaw.
Acrocanthosaurus possessed a powerful bite, generating an anterior force of 8,266 newtons and a posterior force of 16,894 newtons.
The holotype specimen displays a fractured and healed neural spine on the eleventh vertebra alongside an unusual hook-like structure on the third tail vertebra.
The genus Acrocanthosaurus was named and described by American paleontologists J. Willis Stovall and Wann Langston Jr. in 1950.
Definite Acrocanthosaurus fossils have been found in formations across Texas, Oklahoma, Wyoming, Arizona, Utah, and Maryland.
Acrocanthosaurus forelimbs did not touch the ground and were used for hunting rather than walking, consistent with non-avian theropods where arms are not used for locomotion.

The Acrocanthosaurus arm could not reach a vertical position when swinging down but could swing up to 9 degrees above horizontal, while the shoulder allowed the arm to retract 109 degrees from the vertical but not make a full circle.
When accounting for lost Harris lines, Acrocanthosaurus likely needed 18 to 24 years to reach maturity.
Acrocanthosaurus is classified within the superfamily Allosauroidea and the infraorder Tetanurae, with most studies placing it in the family Carcharodontosauridae.

Brain reconstruction supports the hypothesis that Acrocanthosaurus was a carcharodontosaurid, showing similarities to Allosaurus and Sinraptor rather than other theropods, and resembling those of Carcharodontosaurus and Giganotosaurus.

Acrocanthosaurus lived during the Early Cretaceous (Barremian) and Late Cretaceous (Cenomanian) periods, existing between 125 and 99.6 million years ago, specifically from the Aptian to Cenomanian stages between 121.4 and 93.9 million years ago.
The environment where Acrocanthosaurus fossils were found was a large floodplain draining into a shallow inland sea.

J. Willis Stovall and Wann Langston Jr. first assigned Acrocanthosaurus to Antrodemidae, but Alfred Sherwood Romer transferred it to the wastebasket taxon Megalosauridae in 1956, while an ongoing debate exists regarding its evolutionary relationships with some scientists classifying it as an allosaurid and others as a carcharodontosaurid.

Large theropod footprints found in Texas may belong to Acrocanthosaurus, though no direct link to skeletal remains has been confirmed, and it is debated whether the Glen Rose trackways represent a pack of Acrocanthosaurus stalking sauropods as other explanations exist and the hypothesis is difficult to prove.
Researchers suggest that differences between specimens may indicate a need to reexamine North American carcharodontosaurid material, potentially revealing greater diversity than previously thought.
